title: Integration of split semisimple rational Lie modules with their weight lattice
statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra, def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], and let $\mathfrak h$ be a maximal abelian subalgebra whose adjoint action is diagonalizable over $\mathbf Q$. Let $\Phi$ be the nonzero adjoint weights, and let $h_\alpha\in[\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}]$ be normalized by $\alpha(h_\alpha)=2$. Put $P=\{\mu\in\mathfrak h^\vee:\mu(h_\alpha)\in\mathbf Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$. There exist an affine $\mathbf Q$-group scheme $G$ [def-sc-group-scheme], a split maximal torus $T\subseteq G$, and a Lie isomorphism $j:\mathfrak g\simeq\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ carrying $\mathfrak h$ onto $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$, with the following properties. Here $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ is the tangent space at the identity of $H$, equivalently the kernel of $H(\mathbf Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2))\to H(\mathbf Q)$ with its tangent-vector operations and commutator Lie bracket; differentials are induced by maps on these infinitesimal points.

The group $G$ is smooth, connected, semisimple and simply connected: after algebraic closure it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and every surjective homomorphism from a connected semisimple group to $G$ with finite central kernel is an isomorphism. Solvable means that iterated commutator subgroups eventually vanish. The torus $T$ is isomorphic over $\mathbf Q$ to a finite product of $\mathbf G_m$, and is maximal after algebraic closure. Its character and cocharacter lattices are $X=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf G_m,T)$, with the perfect integer pairing defined by $\chi\circ\eta:t\mapsto t^{\langle\chi,\eta\rangle}$. Differentiation $\chi\mapsto d\chi\circ j|_{\mathfrak h}$ identifies $X$ with $P$. The roots of $(G,T)$, the nonzero $T$-weights of the adjoint action on $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, correspond exactly to $\Phi$; for each $\alpha\in\Phi$, $j$ carries $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ onto the $T$-weight space of $\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ of the corresponding root. Their coroots differentiate to the $h_\alpha$, and this identification preserves all root-coroot pairings. The lattices $X,Y$ are finite-rank free abelian, the roots and coroots span their rational spaces and form a finite reduced crystallographic root datum: each root pairs to $2$ with its coroot, the root and dual reflections permute the root-coroot pairs, and proportional roots differ only by sign. The reflection group is finite.

Every finite-dimensional Lie representation of $\mathfrak g$ on a rational vector space $V$ integrates to a unique algebraic-group representation $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ [def-wf-algebraic-representations] whose differential, pulled back by $j$, is the given action. For this action there is a finite direct sum decomposition $V=\bigoplus_{\chi\in X}V_\chi$, where $t$ acts on $V_\chi$ by $\chi(t)$ after every scalar extension; under $X=P$, the space $V_\chi$ is exactly the simultaneous ordinary $\mathfrak h$-eigenspace of weight $d\chi\circ j$. Empty root systems and the zero Lie algebra are allowed.

source.place: Theorems 22.53 and 23.70(a)--(e), printed pp.481 and 507--508; proof of 23.70(d) identifies the split torus through the integral weight grading. The lattice and root comparison is part of its diagram (V,Phi,P(Phi)).

proof.text: Apply the split root decomposition and the rational base-existence theorem to choose a base $\Delta$. The rational highest-weight theorem supplies the fundamental weights $\omega_i$, a basis $P=\bigoplus_i\mathbf Z\omega_i$, and modules $L(\lambda)$. In particular $P$ is a free lattice of full rank in $\mathfrak h^\vee$. Let $\mathcal C$ be all finite-dimensional rational $\mathfrak g$-modules with their forgetful functor. Kernels and cokernels are the invariant vector-space kernels and cokernels, tensor action is $x(v\otimes w)=xv\otimes w+v\otimes xw$, and dual action is $(xf)(v)=-f(xv)$. These formulas verify the abelian, exact faithful symmetric tensor, and duality hypotheses of the tensor-envelope theorem. A skeleton is obtained by taking actions on $\mathbf Q^n$ for $n\geq0$, a set of matrices in each dimension.

source.place: Theorem 23.70, preceding construction, p.507; root system on pp.503--504.

proof.text: The object $W=\mathbf1\oplus\bigoplus_i L(\omega_i)$ tensor-generates $\mathcal C$. Indeed for $\lambda=\sum n_i\omega_i$ dominant, the tensor product of $n_i$ highest vectors in the $L(\omega_i)$ is nonzero, has weight $\lambda$, and is killed by all positive root spaces. Complete reducibility decomposes the submodule it generates into simple summands. Any nonzero projection of the vector is a highest vector of weight $\lambda$, so highest-weight uniqueness identifies the corresponding summand with $L(\lambda)$. Every simple thus occurs in a tensor word in $W$, and every module is a finite sum of simples. The tensor-envelope theorem consequently gives an affine finite-type group $G=\operatorname{Aut}^{\otimes}(\omega)$, a closed immersion $G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(W)$, and a fibre-preserving tensor equivalence $\mathcal C\simeq\operatorname{Rep}(G)$. No finiteness conclusion is inferred just from the dimension of a Lie algebra.

source.place: Theorem 23.70 construction and proof (a),(b), p.507; Note 9.27, p.173.

proof.text: Send $x\in\mathfrak g$ to the family $(\rho_V(x))_V$. The tensor formulas make this a Lie map $j:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ in the envelope's tangent-family description. It is injective, since its component on the adjoint module is $\operatorname{ad}(x)$ and the centre of a semisimple Lie algebra is zero (the centre is an abelian ideal). The adjoint action is faithful, so the faithful trace-form theorem makes its trace form, the Killing form of $\mathfrak g$, nondegenerate.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(a), p.507; Lie-family description in Lemma 23.69, p.506.

proof.text: Let $D$ be a tangent family. Naturality for the bracket map $\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$ says that $D_{\mathfrak g}$ is a Lie derivation. The inner-derivation leaf gives $x$ with $D_{\mathfrak g}=\operatorname{ad}(x)$. Subtract $j(x)$ to obtain $E$ with $E_{\mathfrak g}=0$. Naturality for the action map $\mathfrak g\otimes V\to V$ now says $E_V\rho_V(y)=\rho_V(y)E_V$. On each simple $V$, classification makes $E_V=c_V\,1$. The Lie algebra is perfect: each simple coroot is $[e_i,f_i]$, these coroots span $\mathfrak h$, and a root vector $z$ is $\alpha(h)^{-1}[h,z]$ for some $h$ with $\alpha(h)\ne0$. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_V(y))=0$, since traces of matrix commutators vanish. Choose a basis of the simple $V$ of dimension $n>0$ and let $a:V^{\otimes n}\to\mathbf Q$ be the determinant multilinear form. In the sum $\sum_i a(v_1,\ldots,Av_i,\ldots,v_n)$, off-diagonal entries of $A$ give repeated columns and vanish, while the diagonal entries sum to $\operatorname{Tr}(A)a(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. Hence $a$ is a Lie-intertwiner to the trivial module. Tensor naturality gives $0=E_{\mathbf Q}a=a E_{V^{\otimes n}}=n c_V a$; as $a$ is nonzero, $c_V=0$ in $\mathbf Q$. Naturality for inclusions of simple summands then gives $E=0$ on every module. Therefore $j$ is surjective and is a Lie isomorphism.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(a), p.507; expanded tangent-family argument using inner derivations and determinants.

proof.text: Smoothness follows from Cartier's theorem for the finite-type $G$. Under the reconstructed tensor equivalence, its differentiation, pulled back by $j$, is exactly the original Lie action, because the component of $j(x)$ at $V$ is $\rho_V(x)$. Hence every rational Lie action has an algebraic integration on its very same vector space. For uniqueness let $r$ be any algebraic representation on $V$ whose differential, pulled back by $j$, is $\rho_V$. Essential surjectivity of the equivalence gives an object $V_1$ of $\mathcal C$ and a $G$-isomorphism $\varphi$ from $r$ to the tautological action on $V_1$. Differentiation is a functor, so $\varphi$ intertwines $\rho_V$ with $\rho_{V_1}$; hence $\varphi$ is a morphism $V\to V_1$ of $\mathcal C$, and the tautological functor makes $\varphi$ a $G$-map from the tautological action on $V$. Therefore $r_A(g)=\varphi^{-1}g_{V_1}\varphi$ is the tautological action of $g$ on $A\otimes V$, for every $A$ and $g\in G(A)$. In particular every zero-differential representation of $G$ is trivial. The connectedness test shows that $G$ is geometrically connected, and the semisimple-Lie converse, applied to $j$, makes $G$ semisimple. Over the algebraic closure this semisimple group is reductive by the Borel-pair structure theorem.

Set $T=D_{\mathbf Q}(P)=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Q[P]$. The character antiduality identifies $X^*(T)$ with $P$; choosing the basis $\omega_i$ identifies $T$ with $\mathbf G_m^r$. The Lie-module classification decomposes every $V$ into ordinary $\mathfrak h$-eigenspaces $V_\mu$, $\mu\in P$. Give each $V_\mu$ the $T$-action of character $\mu$. Lie-intertwiners preserve these eigenspaces, tensor weights add and the unit has weight zero, so for every algebra $A$ a point $t\in T(A)$ gives a tensor-natural automorphism on all $A\otimes V$. The envelope's representing property yields $i:T\to G$. Each $\omega_i$ occurs as the highest weight in $L(\omega_i)\subset W$. In a weight basis of $W$ the composite $T\to G\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ is diagonal; its coordinate pullback contains $e^{\omega_i}$ and $e^{-\omega_i}$, since both a matrix and its inverse have regular entries on $\operatorname{GL}(W)$. These generate $\mathbf Q[P]$, so the composite coordinate map is surjective and so is $\mathbf Q[G]\to\mathbf Q[P]$. Thus $i$ is a closed immersion.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), pp.507--508; split torus and grading in 12.13, p.235.

proof.text: A tangent point of $T$ sends $e^\mu$ to $1+\varepsilon\mu(h)$, with $h\in\mathfrak h$: this follows by specifying the coefficients on the basis $\omega_i$ and extending multiplicatively. Its action on $V_\mu$ is $1+\varepsilon\mu(h)$, so $di$ identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$ with $j(\mathfrak h)$. In these coordinates $d\chi\circ j|_{\mathfrak h}=\mu$ for $\chi=\chi_\mu$, giving exactly $X=P$, with no scalar multiple. If a geometric torus $S$ contains $T$, then $\operatorname{Lie}(S)$ centralizes $j(\mathfrak h)$. The split root decomposition, extended to the algebraic closure, has zero-weight space exactly $\mathfrak h$, so $\operatorname{Lie}(S)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)$. Apply smooth-subgroup tangent generation with ambient $S$ and the single subgroup $T$: it gives $S=T$. Thus $T$ is geometrically maximal.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), p.508; maximality expanded from the Cartan centralizer.

proof.text: For the adjoint module, the same grading gives $\operatorname{Lie}(G)=j(\mathfrak h)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}j(\mathfrak g_\alpha)$ with torus characters $\alpha$. It is the group adjoint representation: differentiation of $\operatorname{Ad}$ pulled back by $j$ is $\operatorname{ad}$, so uniqueness from step 5 identifies it with the reconstructed adjoint module. Thus its nonzero torus weights and weight spaces are exactly the stated roots and root spaces. Tangent calculus identifies $\operatorname{Lie}(G_{\overline{\mathbf Q}})$ with $\overline{\mathbf Q}\otimes\operatorname{Lie}(G)$, so the same decomposition holds over the algebraic closure. There apply rank-one reflections to $(G,T)$. By tangent calculus the differential of $v_\alpha:\operatorname{SL}_2\to G_\alpha\subseteq G$ preserves brackets and composites. For the standard $e,f,h$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ put $e'=dv_\alpha(e)$, $f'=dv_\alpha(f)$, $h'=dv_\alpha(h)=d\alpha^\vee(1)$. Then $h'\in\operatorname{Lie}(T)=j(\mathfrak h)$, $e'$ spans the root space $j(\mathfrak g_\alpha)$, $[e',f']=h'$, and $\alpha(h')=\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$, since $t\mapsto t^n$ has differential $n$. Write $f'=f'_0+\sum_\beta f'_\beta$ in the root decomposition (transported by $j$). Then $[e',f'_0]=-\alpha(f'_0)e'$ lies in the $\alpha$-space and $[e',f'_\beta]$ in the $(\alpha+\beta)$-space; as $[e',f']=h'$ lies in $j(\mathfrak h)$, all other components vanish and $h'=[e',f'_{-\alpha}]\in j([\mathfrak g_\alpha,\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}])$. The bracket line and the normalization $\alpha(h')=2$ characterize $h_\alpha$ uniquely, so $d\alpha^\vee(1)=j(h_\alpha)$. The cocharacter is defined over $\mathbf Q$: for a split torus its integer coordinates are $\mu\mapsto\mu(h_\alpha)$, so the geometric cocharacter is the one already given over $\mathbf Q$ by these coordinates.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), p.508; rank-one coroot convention in Theorem 21.11, pp.428--430.

proof.text: Identify $Y$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(P,\mathbf Z)$ by character antiduality; its basis dual to the $\omega_i$ gives the perfect integer pairing. Step 8 identifies the coroots with $h_\alpha$. Both root and coroot families span the rational spaces by the split Lie root theorem. Its root-coroot evaluations, normalization, reducedness and reflection permutation formulas are therefore the same for $(X,\Phi,Y,\Phi^\vee)$. The formulas preserve $P$: evaluation of $s_\alpha(\mu)$ on any $h_\beta$ equals evaluation of $\mu$ on the corresponding reflected coroot and is integral. They preserve the dual lattice too. The finite rational reflection group is consequently the lattice reflection group. This proves all asserted root-datum properties and pairings.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), p.508; its diagram interpreted by the full weight lattice.

proof.text: Work over an algebraic closure. The Borel-pair theorem gives some pair $(B_0,T_0)$. Torus conjugacy gives $gT_0g^{-1}=T$, so $gB_0g^{-1}$ is a Borel containing our specified $T$. Let $f:H\to G$ be a surjection from a connected semisimple group with finite central kernel. The semisimple central-isogeny theorem makes it faithfully flat, and Borel/root compatibility gives a maximal torus $T_H=f^{-1}(T)$ containing the kernel and preserving root-coroot pairings. On torus characters $f^*:P\hookrightarrow X^*(T_H)$ has finite cokernel, by diagonalizable character duality and finiteness of its kernel. Identify their rational spaces through $f^*$. Every $\xi\in X^*(T_H)$ has integral evaluation on all coroots, so $\xi\in P$; conversely $P$ is already included. Thus $f^*$ is an isomorphism. Character duality makes $T_H\to T$ an isomorphism and its kernel trivial. Hence $\ker f=1$. The affine faithfully flat map $f$ is an fpqc cover. The identity map on its source, viewed as a local inverse, agrees on the double overlap: two lifts of the same point differ by an element of the trivial kernel. Representable fpqc descent glues it to an inverse on $G$; the two composite identities hold after this cover and hence hold by the uniqueness clause of the same descent theorem. This proves geometric simply-connectedness; it also proves the stated assertion for isogenies defined over $\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(e), p.508, via Proposition 23.29, p.493; full lattice argument written explicitly.

proof.text:
For every integrated module, restriction to $T$ is precisely its original $P$-grading, by the construction of $i$ in step 6. The diagonalizable representation theorem gives a finite direct sum of actual character spaces, with the indicated character action after every scalar extension. Differentiating shows that the character space $V_\mu$ is contained in its ordinary $\mathfrak h$-eigenspace. Conversely if $v=\sum v_
u$ is an eigenvector of weight $\mu$, then $(
u(h)-\mu(h))v_
u=0$ for every $h$; distinct rational linear forms are separated by some $h$, so only $v_\mu$ can remain. This proves equality, not just containment. For $\mathfrak g=0$ the root decomposition gives $\mathfrak h=0$ and $P=0$; $\mathcal C$ is vector spaces, its tensor automorphism group is $1$ (naturality for maps $\mathbf Q	o V$ fixes every vector), $T=1$, and all assertions reduce to the unique trivial action. The zero module is the empty direct sum.
